newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Europe defined contribution pensions seen growing.
newsitem.headline: Europe defined contribution pensions seen growing.

text.p: European pension funds will turn increasingly to defined contribution programmes, as governments seek a way out from the crushing costs of state-funded pensions.
"Over time defined contribution will be the highest growth area," Robert Flater, president of Fidelity International Retirement Group told the European Asset Management Conference on Wednesday.

In Britain alone, defined pension schemes are expected to hit more than $200 billion in assets under management in 2000, from under $50 billion today. That figure could top $500 billion by 2005, according to Fidelity.

Defined contribution schemes, under which employers and employees make fixed contributions to a pension fund, can be fomented by governments to provide an alternative safety net to state-funded schemes.
"Demographic trends are threatening many state systems' solvency and survival," Flater told Reuters, "Pay-as-you-go systems will go bankrupt."
Low birth rates and an ageing population mean that many European nations will soon have too few workers supporting too many retirees, he said.
Britain has already seen strong growth in the defined benefit sector, with assets under management doubling in the past two years to about six percent, according to Flater.

Even the Netherlands, which enjoy one of Europe's most robust state pension systems, will see the need to encourage defined benefit schemes, according to Frank Kusse, head of institutional services at ABN AMRO Asset Management.
"The government is withdrawing and it wants companies to offer employees flexible systems," Kusse told Reuters.

The Netherlands has historically had almost no defined contribution schemes, but many of the country's top asset managers are currently working in partnership with companies to develop them, Kusse said.

The push to European monetary union will add impetus to the defined benefit movement, as governments are faced with the hard choice of failing deficit criteria or backing away from underfunded state pensions.
"Unfunded state pension liabilities can be one of the large triggers to kick you into a soft euro," Flater said.
To be sure, it remains to be seen if much of Europe will have the political will to put the onus for retirement savings on companies and individuals.
Sunday's victory by the left in France is a case in point.
"France will have a delaying effect," Flater said. "Two or three months ago we would have thought France was the best bet to develop a US-style defined contribution system. All bets are off now."
But Flater thinks that it is just a matter of time before Europe seizes on the benefits of defined contribution schemes.
He points to the US, where their rapid growth has taken defined contribution schemes to about 33 percent of the $3.2 trillion under management.
"There is a high correlation between the countries that have high savings rates and those that have fully funded pension schemes," he said.
